benchmarks.note: treat with caution: the headline figure for Corolla 'tie rod replacement' is $1,401-$1,640 with no parts/labor split, model year or scope shown, far above every other source. RepairPal's Nissan Titan page (https://repairpal.com/estimator/nissan/titan/tie-rod-replacement-cost) shows the same pattern: a $2,354-$2,617 headline next to per-model-year figures of $191-$242. finding: The live range of $170-$900 is about right at the bottom but too wide at the top for one outer tie rod end. Built totals for one outer end, parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr (the national middle labor rate used for these checks), with no alignment: economy 2015 Corolla about $87-$232 (0.5-1.0 hr); midsize 2016 CR-V about $79-$215 (0.5-1.0 hr); truck 2016 F-150 about $93-$313 (0.5-1.0 hr); luxury 2015 BMW 328i about $108-$272 (0.5-1.0 hr). The part is cheap ($19-$48 aftermarket, $55-$153 at manufacturer list) and the job is short. The bottom: nearly every quote adds a wheel alignment, because the toe setting is disturbed. Manufacturer bulletins allow 0.4 hr (Acura), 0.7-1.1 hr (Mazda) and 1.0 hr (FCA) for an alignment, and one guide prices it at $100-$180, so a realistic all-in figure for one side is roughly $180-$500. That makes $170 a fair floor, and two of the benchmarks agree ($150-$400 including alignment; $222-$348). The top: nothing found supports $900 for one outer end. The highest comparable benchmark is $750 including alignment, and our highest built total plus an alignment is about $500. $900 is only reached when both sides, an inner tie rod, or dealer-priced parts and labor are included, so the top should either come down to about $500-$750 or the page should say that the upper end covers both sides or inner and outer together. How solid the labor times are: weak, and confidence stays low. No manufacturer-stated time for an outer tie rod end was found for any of the four example vehicles. Only the truck figures are for the example vehicle itself: parts-seller listings for the F-150 outer end state about 30 minutes (one listing) and about 1 hour (four listings), which are sellers' approximations and not book times. For the Corolla, CR-V and BMW the 0.5-1.0 hr range comes from one mechanic-written guide, supported by a second guide ('less than an hour'). The only manufacturer flat-rate time found for this exact job is Tesla's 0.24 hr for a Model 3; it is shown as a cross-check only and is no longer used as the luxury low end, because it is not a BMW figure and is shorter than a shop would normally bill. Recall bulletins from Nissan (1.9 hr) and Mazda (about 2.0 hr) cover both inner or complete tie rods on both sides, a bigger job, and are shown only as cross-checks. A second look on 2026-11-20 searched manufacturer bulletins and recall dealer letters from Honda/Acura, Hyundai/Kia, Nissan, Mazda, GM, FCA, Ford, Subaru and Jaguar Land Rover and found no operation for replacing one outer tie rod end on any vehicle in the economy, midsize or luxury class, so no example vehicle was changed and no number moved. What turned up only brackets the job: GM allows 0.3 hr to disconnect, refit and retorque one outer tie rod joint on a 2024 Malibu with nothing replaced, and Mazda allows 0.8 hr for an operation that replaces the driver's-side tie rod (inner joint) on a Mazda3, Mazda6 or CX-5 with alignment extra, though that bulletin does not describe what the time covers. Both sit comfortably around the 0.5-1.0 hr used here, as does a UK marketplace's 'around 1 hour'. Still weak: economy, midsize and luxury each rest on one general mechanic-written guide, and three of the four classes (six of eight hour figures) are not for the example vehicle. Rusted or seized adjusting sleeves and jam nuts add time.
extras: A quote almost always adds a wheel alignment (manufacturer bulletins allow 0.4-1.1 hr; one guide puts it at $100-$180). Shops often recommend doing the other side at the same time, which doubles parts and adds less than double the labor. Also common: an inner tie rod and its rack boot if the inner joint is worn too (a longer job), a new jam nut, castle nut or cotter pin, extra labor for a rusted or seized tie rod, a steering and suspension inspection or diagnosis fee, a steering angle sensor reset on newer cars, shop supplies and sales tax.
